tent.name: Tent
tent.desc: Where it starts. Energy max 20; each Rest answer gives 5 energy.

well_1.name: Old Bucket
well_1.desc: All that is left: a small dented bucket. Carry water from the wild pond: 2 💧 a trip for 1 ⚡. Holds 8.

ruins_workshop.name: Clear the old workshop
ruins_workshop.desc: What is left of the old workshop is in the way: clear it away before anything new can stand here. It gives stones back.

road_1.name: Muddy track
road_1.desc: The old road is mud and potholes. Only the seed seller with her basket gets through.

road_1b.name: Lay brushwood over the mud
road_1b.desc: Bundles of brushwood over the worst mud: the seed seller's handcart gets through a little more often.

road_2.name: Fill the potholes
road_2.desc: Stones and sticks in the worst holes: carts can come now — the timber & stone seller, the seed cart and the book cart.

basket.name: Basket
basket.desc: Holds up to 10 of each item.

hands.name: Hands
hands.desc: Plant, harvest and pull weeds by hand.

rock.name: Rock
rock.desc: Good enough to knock simple things together.

bucket.name: Watering Scoop
bucket.desc: Waters the plants. Plants use their full water cost.

seed_1.name: Seed Merchant
seed_1.desc: Always there, always takes coins. Wheat and carrot seeds.

land_start.name: One cleared patch
land_start.desc: The rest of the field is overgrown.

crop_wheat.name: Wheat
crop_wheat.desc: The backbone crop: food, feed, flour and straw.

campfire.name: Campfire
campfire.desc: First build. With the Tin Pot: porridge and soup.

d_porridge.name: Feed the travelling merchant
d_porridge.desc: She shares news — and opens her cart properly.

raw_1.name: Raw Materials · timber & stone
raw_1.desc: Safety valve for basic building materials.

crop_clover.name: Clover
crop_clover.desc: Cheap, quick fodder. Its flowers feed bees.

present_onion.name: A present for the seed cart
present_onion.desc: Give the seed seller two bowls of porridge — next time she brings onion sets.

clear_thistles.name: Clear the thistles (2 patches)
clear_thistles.desc: Takes 4 steps, one tap each; every step gives something back. After the first 2 steps the 2 patches can be planted; the other steps make them better (bigger harvests, fewer weeds).

clear_weeds.name: Pull the weeds (2 patches)
clear_weeds.desc: Takes 5 steps, one tap each; every step gives something back. After the first 2 steps the 2 patches can be planted; the other steps make them better (bigger harvests, fewer weeds).

stone_knife.name: Stone Knife
stone_knife.desc: Rough chopping. Needed for any recipe that cuts things.

stone_axe.name: Hand Axe
stone_axe.desc: Clears stumps, splits logs into planks, cuts sticks faster.

wooden_shovel.name: Wooden Shovel
wooden_shovel.desc: Pries out rocks and digs beds: field work −10% energy.

clear_rocks.name: Clear the rocks (2 patches)
clear_rocks.desc: Takes 5 steps, one tap each; every step gives something back. After the first 2 steps the 2 patches can be planted; the other steps make them better (bigger harvests, fewer weeds).

clear_stumps.name: Clear the stumps (2 patches)
clear_stumps.desc: Takes 5 steps, one tap each; every step gives something back. After the first 2 steps the 2 patches can be planted; the other steps make them better (bigger harvests, fewer weeds).

chopping_block.name: Chopping Block
chopping_block.desc: A stump to cut on. Salads and bowls (needs a knife).

quern.name: Hand Quern
quern.desc: Two flat stones from the rocky patch grind wheat into flour. Hard work (2 ⚡).

well_2.name: Dig a well
well_2.desc: A stone well right by the house: 4 💧 a trip, holds 24.

well_3.name: Well · winch
well_3.desc: A winch and a bigger bucket: 6 💧 a trip, holds 36.

animal_chicken.name: Chickens
animal_chicken.desc: Eat any grain (wheat, oats, sunflower seeds, linseed, mash), need water and nest straw, lay an egg every question — and drop a feather now and then.

scarecrow_1.name: Stick Scarecrow
scarecrow_1.desc: Shoots fierce looks at birds and rabbits (removes 0.6 pests per question) and they leave the seeds alone: planting costs half the energy.

d_veg_soup.name: Soup for the village
d_veg_soup.desc: The village notices you. Two new merchants arrive.

seed_3.name: Seed Merchant · stall
seed_3.desc: Potato, lettuce, beans and beet seeds.

spice_1.name: Spice Merchant
spice_1.desc: Salt. (Barter idea: also asks for 1 onion per salt.)

pet_bunny.name: Bunny comes home
pet_bunny.desc: Pet 1 (default name Pip; the player can rename). Bonus: every carrot harvest gives +1 carrot.

wild_edge.name: Field Edge & Woods
wild_edge.desc: Always open: gather sticks, pick stones, pull wild weeds. What you gather comes at once; each spot refills after a Time Quiz question. Costs energy, never coins.

patch_dug.name: Dug beds
patch_dug.desc: Loosen the soil: 2 plants of the same crop fit in one patch.

patch_edged.name: Stick edging
patch_edged.desc: A woven stick border keeps weeds out: weeds grow 20% slower.

patch_raised.name: Raised log beds
patch_raised.desc: 3 plants per patch. Every plant beyond 2 needs 1 fertilizer point per planting (wood ash at first).

gathering_basket.name: Gathering Basket
gathering_basket.desc: Carry more per trip: gathering takes 2 loads per tap (2× energy), and −25% energy.

straw_bed.name: Straw Bed
straw_bed.desc: Sleep better: +1 energy per Rest answer.

whetstone.name: Whetstone
whetstone.desc: Sharp blades: cutting and wood work −10% energy.

carrying_yoke.name: Carrying Yoke
carrying_yoke.desc: Two buckets on a pole: +2 💧 every trip to the pond, and planting is easier.

lucky_horseshoe.name: Tom's lucky horseshoe

sq_lost_goat.name: Granny Maud's goat ran off
sq_lost_goat.desc: Reward: a picture for the album — Granny Maud laughing, hugging her muddy goat on the rope you found it with.

reward.picture: Granny Maud laughing, hugging her muddy goat on the rope you found it with

straw_hat.name: Straw Hat
straw_hat.desc: Shade from the sun: energy max +2.

sq_twins_porridge.name: Porridge for the hungry twins
sq_twins_porridge.desc: Reward: a picture for the album — The twins beaming, each holding a bowl of your porridge (some on their noses).

reward.picture: The twins beaming, each holding a bowl of your porridge (some on their noses)

sq_miller_basket.name: The miller's daughter needs a basket
sq_miller_basket.desc: Reward: a picture for the album — Ella twirling with your new basket full of flowers.

reward.picture: Ella twirling with your new basket full of flowers

brass_bell.name: Ella's brass bell
brass_bell.desc: A little bell on the field gate: it jingles in the wind and the birds don't like it.

book_basics.name: The Little Farm Book
book_basics.desc: Free. Was already in the box in the tent: planting, fire, rope, the first tools.

book_village.name: Village Crafts
book_village.desc: Timber, clay, walls and roofs — how the village builds.

book_cart.name: Book Cart
book_cart.desc: Comes with the travelling merchant. Sells the books your library has room for.

library_box.name: Book box in the tent
library_box.desc: Holds 2 books. The Little Farm Book was already in it.

k_wheat.name: Growing wheat
k_wheat.desc: Opening the book. A seed needs soil, water and time.
k_wheat.topic: Opening the book. A seed needs soil, water and time; wheat seeds are sown in loose soil, watered, then the stalks grow, turn golden and are cut; each stalk gives grain (to eat or sow) and straw.
k_wheat.page: Every seed needs three things to grow: soil, water and time. Farmers sow wheat seeds in loose soil and water them. The green stalks grow tall, turn golden, and then they are cut. Each stalk gives grain, to eat or to sow again, and a dry stem called straw.

questions.q: What three things does a seed need to grow?
questions.why: With soil, water and enough time, a seed can sprout and grow.

questions.q: How can you tell your wheat is ready to cut?
questions.why: Wheat turns golden when the grain is ripe and ready to harvest.

questions.q: What two things does each wheat stalk give you?
questions.why: The top gives grain to eat or sow, and the dry stem is straw.

k_fire.name: A safe little fire
k_fire.desc: Fire needs three things: fuel, air and heat (fire triangle). Build it inside a ring of stones, start with dry twigs before thicker sticks, never leave it alone, put it out with water or soil.
k_fire.topic: Fire needs three things: fuel, air and heat (fire triangle). Build it inside a ring of stones, start with dry twigs before thicker sticks, never leave it alone, put it out with water or soil.
k_fire.page: A fire needs three things: fuel to burn, air, and heat. Build it inside a ring of stones, and light small dry twigs before you add thicker sticks. Never leave a fire alone. To put it out, pour on water or cover it with soil, which keeps the air away.

questions.q: What three things does every fire need?
questions.why: Take away the fuel, the air or the heat, and the fire goes out.

questions.q: Your big sticks won't catch fire. What should you light first?
questions.why: Small dry twigs catch fire easily and then help the bigger sticks burn.

questions.q: Why does covering a fire with soil put it out?
answers: The soil keeps the air away
The soil makes the fire hotter
The soil burns up like fuel
questions.why: A fire needs air, so covering it with soil makes it go out.

k_roots.name: Roots you can eat
k_roots.desc: Carrots and onions are plants whose roots/bulbs we eat.
k_roots.topic: Carrots and onions are plants whose roots/bulbs we eat; the green leaves above ground make food from sunlight; they grow slower than leafy plants; pull them when the top is big.
k_roots.page: With carrots and onions, we eat the part under the ground: a carrot's root and an onion's round bulb. Their green leaves above the ground use sunlight to make food for the plant. They grow more slowly than leafy plants like lettuce. Pull them up when the green tops are big.

questions.q: Which part of a carrot do we eat?
questions.why: The orange part we eat is the carrot's root, which grows underground.

questions.q: What do the green leaves of a carrot do?
answers: Soak up rain for the root
questions.why: Leaves use sunlight to make food for the whole plant, even the root.

questions.q: How can you tell your carrots are ready to pull?
answers: The leaves are still small and new
questions.why: Big green tops mean the root below has had time to grow big too.

k_rope.name: Twisting rope from fibres
k_rope.desc: Rope is made by twisting plant fibres (from tough weed stems, flax, or straw) into strands and twisting the strands together the other way so the rope does not unwind.
k_rope.topic: Rope is made by twisting plant fibres (from tough weed stems, flax, or straw) into strands and twisting the strands together the other way so the rope does not unwind; more strands = stronger rope.
k_rope.page: Rope is made from fibres, the thin, tough threads inside plant stems like flax or straw. First you twist the fibres into strands. Then you twist the strands together the other way, so the rope does not unwind. The more strands you use, the stronger the rope.

questions.q: Why twist the strands together the other way?
answers: So the rope does not unwind
questions.why: Twisting the opposite way locks the strands, so the rope holds together.

questions.q: You need rope to lift a heavy bucket. What makes it stronger?
questions.why: Each extra strand shares the pull, so the rope gets stronger.

questions.q: What is rope made from?
answers: Thin twigs tied together in knots
questions.why: Fibres from plants like flax or straw are twisted to make rope.

k_tools.name: Stone tools
k_tools.desc: The first tools: a sharp flake of stone becomes a knife.
k_tools.topic: The first tools: a sharp flake of stone becomes a knife; a stone head tied (hafted) to a stick handle with rope becomes an axe; handles make tools stronger by leverage; people used stone tools for a very long time (Stone Age).
k_tools.page: The first tools were made of stone. A sharp flake chipped off a stone makes a knife. Tie a stone to a wooden handle with rope to make an axe; the handle lets you swing much harder. People used stone tools for a very, very long time, called the Stone Age.

questions.q: Why tie a stone axe head onto a handle?
answers: So you can swing much harder
So the stone stays sharp forever
questions.why: A handle works like a longer arm, so each swing hits much harder.

questions.q: How were the very first knives made?
answers: From a sharp flake of stone
From melted iron poured into a mould
questions.why: People chipped a sharp flake off a stone and used it to cut.

questions.q: What do we call the long time when people used stone tools?
questions.why: People used stone tools for so long that we call it the Stone Age.

k_weeds.name: Why weeds come back
k_weeds.desc: Weeds are wild plants that grow where we do not want them.
k_weeds.topic: Weeds are wild plants that grow where we do not want them; they steal water, light and food from crops; their seeds blow in and wait in the soil; pulling them with roots stops them regrowing; borders and mulch help.
k_weeds.page: Weeds are wild plants that grow where we don't want them. They steal water, light and food from our crops. Their seeds blow in on the wind and can wait in the soil for years. Pull weeds out with their roots, and use a border or a cover of straw to keep new ones away.

questions.q: Why are weeds bad for your crops?
answers: They steal water, light and food
They make the soil much too loose
questions.why: Weeds take the water, light and food that your crops need.

questions.q: You pulled a weed, but it grew back. What went wrong?
answers: Its roots stayed in the soil
You pulled it on a sunny day
questions.why: If the roots stay in the ground, the weed can grow again.

questions.q: Your bed is clean now. How can you keep new weeds away?
answers: Water the bare soil every day
questions.why: A straw cover or a border stops many weed seeds from growing.

k_water.name: Water and the well
k_water.desc: A well reaches water stored underground (groundwater) that came from rain soaking into the soil.
k_water.topic: A well reaches water stored underground (groundwater) that came from rain soaking into the soil; a deeper shaft reaches more water; a winch (a roller with a handle) makes lifting the bucket easier.
k_water.page: Rain soaks down through the soil and is stored deep underground. This water is called groundwater. A well is a deep hole that reaches it, and a deeper well reaches more water. A winch, which is a roller with a handle, makes lifting the heavy bucket much easier.

questions.q: Where does the water in a well come from?
answers: Rain that soaked into the ground
The sea, flowing under the farm
Ice melting at the bottom of the hole
questions.why: Rain soaks into the soil and collects deep underground as groundwater.

questions.q: Your well keeps running dry. What could help?
questions.why: A deeper well reaches more of the water stored underground.

questions.q: What does a winch help you do?
questions.why: Turning the winch handle winds up the rope, so lifting is easier.

k_soil.name: Loose soil, happy roots
k_soil.desc: Roots need air and water in the soil.
k_soil.topic: Roots need air and water in the soil; digging loosens hard soil so roots can grow deep and more plants fit in one bed; worms also loosen soil; stamping on beds packs it hard again.
k_soil.page: Roots need air and water in the soil to grow. Digging breaks up hard soil, so roots can grow deep and more plants fit in one bed. Worms help too, because their tunnels loosen the soil. But stamping on a bed packs it hard again.

questions.q: Why do roots grow better in loose soil?
answers: Loose soil is warmer in winter
questions.why: Loose soil has room for air and water, and roots can push down deep.

questions.q: Which little animal helps loosen the soil?
questions.why: Worms dig tunnels as they move, which loosens the soil.

questions.q: Your friend keeps walking on your bed. What happens to the soil?
questions.why: Feet squeeze the soil tight, so roots struggle to grow.

k_ash.name: Ash feeds the soil
k_ash.desc: Wood ash from a fire contains minerals (like potassium) that plants need.
k_ash.topic: Wood ash from a fire contains minerals (like potassium) that plants need; sprinkling a little on beds feeds crops; plants growing close together need more food (fertilizer); too much ash is not good either.
k_ash.page: Wood ash from the fire holds minerals, like potassium, that plants need. Sprinkle a little on your beds to feed your crops. Plants growing close together need extra food, called fertilizer. But be careful: too much ash can harm plants.

questions.q: Why sprinkle wood ash on your beds?
answers: It has minerals that feed plants
It helps the soil hold on to rain
questions.why: Ash holds minerals like potassium, which help plants grow.

questions.q: Your bed is packed with plants. What do they need more of?
questions.why: Many plants close together share the soil's food, so they need extra.

questions.q: How much ash should you put on a bed?
questions.why: A little ash feeds plants, but too much can harm them.

k_chickens.name: Keeping hens
k_chickens.desc: Hens eat grain and seeds, drink water every day, need a dry coop with straw to sleep safe from foxes, and lay eggs.
k_chickens.topic: Hens eat grain and seeds, drink water every day, need a dry coop with straw to sleep safe from foxes, and lay eggs; a hen does not need a rooster to lay eggs; they also scratch for bugs.
k_chickens.page: Hens eat grain and seeds, and they scratch the ground to find bugs. They need fresh water every day and a dry coop with straw, where they sleep safe from foxes. Hens lay eggs, and a hen does not need a rooster to lay them.

questions.q: Where should your hens sleep at night?
answers: In a dry coop with straw
Out in the open field all night
questions.why: A dry coop keeps hens cosy and safe from foxes.

questions.q: Do hens need a rooster to lay eggs?
answers: No, hens lay eggs on their own
Yes, every egg needs a rooster
questions.why: A hen lays eggs whether or not there is a rooster.

questions.q: Why do hens scratch at the ground?
questions.why: Hens scratch the soil to find tasty bugs and seeds.

k_birds.name: Birds, seeds and scarecrows
k_birds.desc: Birds love freshly sown seeds and rabbits nibble young plants.
k_birds.topic: Birds love freshly sown seeds and rabbits nibble young plants; a scarecrow that looks like a person frightens birds; moving or flapping things work better; a fence keeps rabbits out; more plants attract more pests.
k_birds.page: Birds love to eat freshly sown seeds, and rabbits nibble young plants. A scarecrow looks like a person, so it frightens birds, but things that flap or move scare them even better. A fence keeps rabbits out. Remember: the more plants you grow, the more hungry visitors come.

questions.q: Which scarecrow will keep birds away best?
questions.why: Moving, flapping things scare birds better than a scarecrow that never moves.

questions.q: Rabbits keep nibbling your young plants. What helps most?
questions.why: A fence stops rabbits from reaching your plants.

questions.q: You planted twice as many crops. What should you expect?
answers: Fewer birds and rabbits than before
questions.why: More plants mean more food, so more hungry visitors come.

k_grinding.name: Grinding grain into flour
k_grinding.desc: Flour is grain ground into powder between two stones (a quern, later a mill).
k_grinding.topic: Flour is grain ground into powder between two stones (a quern, later a mill); the hard outside (bran) and the inside get crushed; it takes a lot of turning by hand; bread and pancakes need flour.
k_grinding.page: Flour is grain that has been ground into powder. You crush the grain between two heavy stones called a quern; later, people built mills to do it. The hard outside of the grain, called bran, and the soft inside both get crushed. It takes lots of turning by hand, but then you can make bread and pancakes.

questions.q: How is grain turned into flour?
answers: It is crushed between two stones
It is soaked in water for many days
It is dried in the sun
questions.why: Two heavy stones grind the grain until it becomes fine powder.

questions.q: What is bran?
answers: The hard outside of the grain
The soft inside of the grain
questions.why: Bran is the tough outer skin of each grain.

questions.q: Why is making flour by hand hard work?
answers: The stone needs lots of turning
The grain has to be boiled first
questions.why: You turn the quern stone again and again to grind the grain.

k_market.name: Fair prices
k_market.desc: Buying and selling: things that take more work or are rare cost more.
k_market.topic: Buying and selling: things that take more work or are rare cost more; selling something you made from cheaper things adds value; a fair price is good for buyer and seller; money is a way to swap work.
k_market.page: At the market, people buy and sell. Things that are rare, or take lots of work to make, cost more. When you turn cheap things into something better, like flour into bread, it is worth more. A fair price is good for the buyer and the seller, and money is just a handy way to swap work.

questions.q: Why does a loaf of bread cost more than its flour?
questions.why: Turning flour into bread takes work, so the bread is worth more.

questions.q: What makes a price fair?
answers: It is good for buyer and seller
The seller gets as much as possible
questions.why: A fair price is good for both people, so both are happy to trade.

questions.q: Only a few people sell honey. Why does it cost a lot?
questions.why: When something is rare, people pay more for the little there is.

stick_fence.name: Rickety Stick Fence

perches.name: Roosting Perches
